tagline.text: One of the largest cave systems in the Philippines, running beneath the forests of Calbiga, Samar

location.label: Location
location.text: Brgy. Panayuran, Calbiga, Samar — inside the Samar Island Natural Park

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱3,500–5,000 (per person, one-day caving package; excludes round-trip transport from Tacloban)

children.text: Langun-Gobingob is a group of 12 caves spread over roughly 2,968 hectares beneath the forests of Calbiga, Samar, and is described as the largest cave system in the Philippines. It is a physically demanding adventure through huge chambers, stalactites, bats and blind fish, and a guide is required.

The Langun-Gobingob Caves are a cave system in the Panayuran area of Calbiga municipality on Samar Island. Also known as Calbiga Cave, the system lies inside the Samar Island Natural Park, and English Wikipedia says it covers roughly 2,968 hectares and contains 12 caves, including Langun, Gobingob, Lurodpon and Bitong Mahangin. Many travel outlets describe it as the largest cave system in the Philippines and one of the notable ones in Southeast Asia. The wording used to compare its size varies from source to source, so it is safest to think of it simply as one of the largest in the country.

This is not a show cave where you switch on the lights and stroll in. After walking down a forest trail to the cave mouth, you enter total darkness and must make your way past headlamp-lit passages, ropes, mud and pools of water. The main chamber of Gobingob is described as about
at its widest, and the main chamber of Langun as about
long and
wide, a scale like an underground cathedral. One outlet calls it the second-largest "cathedral cave" in the world, but that comparison comes from a single source, so treat it as a reference only.

The route most travelers take enters through Gobingob Cave and exits through Langun Cave. Gobingob is the oldest and largest part of the system, and deep inside is a wide space called the "Football Field" because of its size. An underground stream flows through the Football Field, and blind fish and crabs are said to live there. From there you pass the Tita Chamber, with giant chandelier-like stalactites, and continue into Langun, where you can reportedly see large numbers of bats leaving the cave around dusk and a "Guano Mountain" of accumulated bat droppings. There are also stories of an opening in Langun's ceiling that lets daylight shine in.
A day trip takes some mental preparation. From town you ride a motorcycle (habal-habal) to the starting point in Panayuran, then walk about
1 hour
through the forest to the Gobingob viewpoint and entrance, spend about
4 hours
inside the cave, and from the Langun exit climb a steep mountain trail for about
3 hours

back toward town. Travel accounts almost always mention how hard the uphill is, and at least one visitor was injured in a fall on the muddy trail. So this cave is recommended for people who are confident in their fitness and don't mind getting wet and muddy. There is said to be no age limit, but one operator sets a guideline of age 8 and up. The prices and schedules in this guide come mostly from travel accounts and operator listings from 2014 to 2021. Prices differed from source to source and some are old, so only figures that overlap across sources are given as ranges, and the rest is marked "confirm locally." Before you go, be sure to ask the Calbiga tourism office or a local operator about current prices and cave conditions.

This is the central space of Gobingob Cave and part of the oldest and largest section of the system. It is compared to a football field because of its size, and groups also camp and take their lunch break here. An underground stream flows through it, and blind fish and crabs can reportedly be seen.
The main chamber of Langun is described as about
long and

wide, with a very high ceiling. The floor is covered in mud and bat droppings, and sharp stalagmites stand here and there. When you aim your lights at a single spot, you can really sense how vast it is.

blocks.title: Chandelier stalactites of the Tita Chamber

children.text: The Tita Chamber, on the way from Gobingob to Langun, is known for giant stalactites that hang like chandeliers. Your guide will explain them from a safe spot, so look with your eyes only and do not touch.

Inside the cave you may meet bats, cave crickets, crabs, spiders and fish whose eyes have degenerated. One operator says this fish is found only in Samar's caves, but that has not been verified scientifically, so take it as a reference only.
Thousands of bats leaving Langun Cave in the evening are said to be a famous sight. Depending on your schedule you may not see it, so discuss your timing with your guide.
In Gobingob there is reportedly a section where you rope down a wall of about
. Langun is also said to have a vertical descent of about
at its entrance, though the figures differ for what may be the same place. Both sections require a harness and ropes, and the guides and porters handle the equipment and rigging.

The 1-day course passes through from Gobingob to Langun in a single day, while the 2-day/1-night and 3-day/2-night courses add deeper parts of the cave and activities such as rock climbing, rappelling, mud climbing and swimming. If it is your first time, start with the 1-day course.

Before entering the cave, guides reportedly ask guests to touch a rock at the entrance as a sign of respect. Inside the cave, do not relieve yourself; carry waste out in a container, and take all of your trash with you. The caves lie within the Samar Island Natural Park, so these rules must be followed.

children.text: Arrive in Calbiga town, have breakfast at a restaurant and register for the cave through your operator. If you start from Tacloban or Catbalogan, you must set out before dawn.
Ride a motorcycle (habal-habal) to the starting point in Panayuran. One travel account says it took about
1 hour
Walk about
1 hour
along a forest trail from the starting point to the Gobingob viewpoint. Then a downhill walk of about
0.5km
brings you to the cave entrance.
At the entrance, touch the rock as a sign of respect, check your helmet and headlamp, and go in. You pass giant stalagmites and a flowstone formation called "The Stage."
Eat lunch and rest at the Football Field. Look at the blind fish and crabs.
After the roped descent, see the chandeliers of the Tita Chamber and continue into Langun Cave. This stretch is very muddy.

3 hours
back toward the village. Some itineraries include a wash at Mapaso Spring, about
15 minutes

These times are an example condensed from one operator's 2017 trip account and can vary a lot with season, weather and fitness. Including the final motorcycle ride, the trip takes the whole day, so be prepared to arrive late at night.

children.text: Enter through Gobingob and set up camp gear at the Football Field. Afterward, do rock climbing and exploration.
Cross toward Langun, tour the lower water passages and sections that need ropes with your guide, and exit.
Operators say the 3-day/2-night program adds rope descents, mud climbing, potholing (squeezing through narrow openings) and swimming. Confirm the exact itinerary when you book.
There are direct flights from Manila (NAIA) to Daniel Z. Romualdez Airport in Tacloban (TAC). The flight takes about
1 hour 20 minutes
; airlines and schedules change by season, so check when booking.
From the airport, take a jeepney or tricycle to the city, then go on to the bus and van terminal.
At a terminal in Tacloban, take a van bound for Calbiga or a bus heading toward Calbayog. Travel accounts advise getting off at Calbiga Bridge or in the town center.
The distance is given as about
115km
, and the travel time ranges from just over an hour to 3–4 hours depending on the source. Fares do not agree either, so confirm locally.
From Catbalogan, one account says the bus to Calbiga took about
1 hour 30 minutes

items.title: From Calbiga to the cave starting point

children.text: From Calbiga town, take a motorcycle (habal-habal) to the starting point in Panayuran. From there, it is about
1 hour
on foot to the Gobingob viewpoint and entrance.
Most operators offer packages that include transport. To go independently, arrange registration and a guide through the local tourism office or a guide.
The cave entrance is reached on foot from the village road, so it cannot be reached by private car.

Travel outlets recommend the dry season, March to May. Operators run year-round but stop trips in bad weather. Rain makes the forest trail slippery and raises the water in the cave, making it dangerous, so go in the dry season if you can.

One operator in particular warns that the lower section on the Langun side floods completely when water is high. In the rainy season trips may be changed or canceled, so check the weather with your operator before you set out.

Calbiga is a small rural town with few places to stay or eat. Most people stay in Tacloban or Catbalogan and make the trip as a day tour, or the operator arranges registration and breakfast at a restaurant in Calbiga town. Because the day starts early, it is easier to stay in Calbiga or Catbalogan the night before. One traveler wrote that they had breakfast and registered at a native-chicken eatery in Calbiga.

Inside the cave you eat the lunch included in the package, and you bring your own water and snacks. Operators sometimes pack local Samar treats such as binagol. Eateries and lodgings may change with the season and time, so confirm locally.
Going through an operator is the safest option. Many packages include permits, gear, porters and meals, and a minimum of 2 people is required.
Wear trekking shoes with sturdy soles. Avoid slippers and sandals, which can come off in the mud.
Bring long pants, quick-dry clothing and a change of clothes. One traveler says you can leave spare clothes at a restaurant in town.
Bring at least 2 liters of water and carry all your trash back out. Relieving yourself inside the cave is prohibited; use a container and carry it out.
Bring a headlamp and a backup light. Past the entrance the cave is in complete darkness.
A compact waterproof camera is handy. Humidity fogs lenses and you need your hands free. Turn off the flash and do not touch the stalactites.
If you cannot swim, ask for a life vest. There are said to be sections with deep pools.
Bring plenty of cash. One listing states that credit cards are not accepted.
Alcohol, smoking and pets are prohibited.
This is a genuine caving expedition that requires fitness and experience, and the trail and waterways can become dangerous in rain. Go only with a guide.
The forest trail and the cave are slippery with mud and water. One travel writer fell during the hike and hurt a knee.
The lower section on the Langun side is said to flood completely in high water, so do not cross the river when it rains.
There is a warning that a narrow section near the entrance can fill with water and temporarily block the exit. Follow your guide's judgment.
Snakes may be present, but guides say they are harmless if left alone. Do not touch or chase them.
If you are not fit enough, you can turn back at the cave entrance. One traveler advises practicing first on an easier cave nearby.
Prices, schedules and permit procedures can change, so check the latest announcements before you go.
A natural bridge and cave area in Basey, Samar, often mentioned alongside Calbiga as a signature stop for cave travel on Samar Island. It is some distance away, so plan it as a separate outing.
A bridge linking Samar and Leyte that you can see on the way to and from Tacloban.
The gateway city of the Eastern Visayas region with the airport, and the place where vans to Calbiga depart.
